client:
I've been having such a hard time since my grandma passed away last month. I keep expecting to see her when I visit my parents' house, and then it hits me all over again that she's gone. At work, I'll just stare at my computer screen for hours - I can't seem to focus on anything important. 

I don't know if talking about it will really help...the pain just feels so deep and permanent.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're grieving your grandmother's absence, and how those moments of expectation-turned-loss feel especially painful. It makes sense that concentrating at work feels difficult when you're carrying this heavy emotional weight. What comes up for you when you think about whether talking could help ease some of that pain?

client: I don't know if talking will help, honestly. Every time I start thinking about her, I just feel this crushing guilt that I didn't visit more often before she passed. And now when I try to focus at work, random memories pop up and I have to fight back tears at my desk. It's embarrassing.
therapist: I hear how guilt is compounding your grief, and how painful it feels when those memories surface unexpectedly at work. Many people experience this mix of emotions after losing someone important - you're not alone in this. What do you imagine your grandmother would say about those feelings of guilt you're carrying?

client:
I don't know what she'd say... that's part of why I feel so guilty. Maybe she'd be disappointed in me for not visiting more often before she passed. The memories keep popping up at the worst times, like when I'm in meetings, and then I can't focus on anything else. 

It's hard to imagine her perspective because I keep thinking about all the things I should have done differently. The "you're not alone" thing doesn't really help - it just makes me feel worse that other people are going through this too.
therapist: I hear how stuck you feel in this cycle of guilt and painful memories, and how even well-meaning reassurances aren't landing right now. It might help to gently explore what evidence you have about whether your grandmother actually felt disappointed in you - what were her patterns of responding to you throughout your relationship?

client:
I don't know... she never said she was disappointed outright, but I always felt like I fell short of her expectations. She'd give me these long looks when I didn't visit as often as she wanted, or sigh when I talked about my career choices. Maybe I'm just imagining it, but those moments stick with me more than the nice ones. 

It's hard to think about evidence because my brain just keeps going back to the times I messed up or let her down. Like when I missed her birthday that one year because of work.
therapist: It sounds like these moments of perceived disapproval carry more weight in your memory than the affirming ones - our minds often hold onto what feels like evidence of our shortcomings. I wonder if we could gently explore what your grandmother actually *did* say or do that showed she cared about you?

client: I know she did care in her own way...she always made sure I had food when I visited and asked about school. But it's hard to focus on those things when the criticisms stick out so much more. Even now, remembering her saying "you'll never amount to anything" when I got a bad grade makes my chest feel tight.
therapist: I hear how those painful words still create physical tension when you recall them, even while acknowledging her caring actions too. It makes sense that these conflicting memories would create such a complicated grief experience. What do you notice happens in your body when you try to hold space for both these aspects of your relationship?

client: I feel this tightness in my chest whenever I try to think about both sides - the hurtful words and the good times. It's like my body can't decide whether to tense up or relax, so it just stays stuck in this uncomfortable middle ground. Part of me wants to just focus on the good memories, but then I feel guilty for ignoring the pain she caused.
therapist: It sounds like your body is physically reflecting the emotional tension of holding these complex, contradictory memories simultaneously. That discomfort makes complete sense when we're trying to reconcile both love and hurt from someone important to us. What would it feel like to give yourself permission to acknowledge that both these truths can exist at the same time - that grief can hold both gratitude and pain?

client:
I get what you're saying intellectually, but it feels impossible to hold both those feelings at once without getting overwhelmed. When I try to think about the good memories, the hurt just crashes in and ruins everything. It's like my brain can't handle the contradiction. 

I want to believe both can exist together, but it just makes me feel more guilty - like if I acknowledge the love, I'm excusing the hurt, or if I focus on the pain, I'm betraying the good times. It's exhausting.
therapist: I hear how exhausting it feels to wrestle with these conflicting emotions, and how the attempt to hold both creates more guilt rather than relief. This tension between love and hurt is profoundly human, yet so difficult to bear. What would it feel like to temporarily set aside the need to reconcile these feelings, and simply notice them as they come without judgment?

client:
I don't know if I can just notice these feelings without judging them. Every time I feel love for my family, the hurt immediately follows like a wave of guilt. It's like my brain won't let me have one feeling without the other crashing in. 

The idea of setting them aside sounds nice in theory, but in practice it feels impossible - like trying to ignore an alarm blaring in my head. Doesn't that just mean I'm avoiding dealing with the real issues?
therapist: I hear how intertwined these feelings have become for you, and how attempts to simply observe them get overtaken by that familiar wave of guilt. It's not about avoiding the issues, but rather creating enough space so these emotions don't feel so overwhelming when they arise. What would happen if you approached these waves of feeling with curiosity rather than judgment - noticing how they ebb and flow in intensity?

client:
I get what you're saying about curiosity instead of judgment, but it's hard when the guilt feels so immediate and real. When I try to observe my feelings, it's like the guilt just shouts louder, telling me I *should* be feeling bad about this. 

I want to believe I could just watch these emotions come and go, but they don't feel like waves - more like getting hit by a truck every time.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming and visceral this guilt feels - not like passing waves but like sudden, devastating impacts. That intensity makes complete sense when we're grappling with complex grief and unresolved relationships. What would it feel like to acknowledge that guilt's presence without having to believe everything it's telling you in this moment?

client:
I get what you're saying about not believing everything the guilt tells me, but it's hard when the thoughts feel so true in the moment. Like when I remember how I didn't visit my mom enough before she passed, the guilt screams that I was a terrible daughter - and part of me believes that. 

I don't know how to just observe these feelings without getting sucked into them. It's like the guilt has claws that dig in deeper when I try to step back from it.
therapist: I hear how convincing and gripping that guilty voice feels in those painful moments, and how it reinforces this belief about being a "terrible daughter." That intensity makes it incredibly hard to create any distance from those thoughts. What might it look like to gently challenge that narrative by asking what evidence exists that you were actually a caring daughter in other ways?
